title: Up to thirteen hundred prisoners each way, a rising toll in Zaporizhzhia, and Washington denies the Bahrain strike
summary: Ukraine and Russia agree in principle to swap up to thirteen hundred prisoners each with Europe due at the next talks, the toll from Friday's strikes on Zaporizhzhia rises to two dead and fifty injured, US Central Command denies Iran's claim to have destroyed a radar in Bahrain as Trump says no deal with Iran is needed, another tanker is hit in Hormuz, and an Israeli drone strike kills two in Jabaliya.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: Welcome to the ForceFinder Daily Briefing. I'm Avery.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: And I'm Cole. As always, this show is generated automatically from the open-source reporting behind the ForceFinder map. Every story has source links on the globe, so treat us as a guide, not the final word.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: It's Saturday, November fourteenth. After a week of shuttle diplomacy, from Abu Dhabi to Moscow to Dublin, we finally have some numbers on what was agreed.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: The headline is the prisoner exchange. President Zelensky has confirmed an agreement in principle to swap between twelve hundred and thirteen hundred prisoners of war on each side.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: Jared Kushner, one of the American envoys, says Washington is working toward what would be the largest prisoner exchange of the war. There's no date for it yet.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: And the next round of talks is taking shape. It's expected in either the United Arab Emirates or Switzerland. Zelensky has asked Europe to pick its delegates by the end of November.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: So Europe gets its seat. But there's a catch, according to the Institute for the Study of War. It says Kremlin officials accept European participation only as part of Russia's effort to rework Europe's security order.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: And Kyiv Post reports that in its talks with the American envoys, Moscow demanded that NATO go back to its nineteen ninety-seven borders. Add the Institute's assessment from earlier this week, that Putin rejects any demilitarized zone and still wants the parts of four Ukrainian regions his forces haven't taken, and the distance between the sides on the big questions is still enormous.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: The Institute flagged something else worth knowing about. There's a temporary, local ceasefire in the town of Kostiantynivka, which has been one of the busiest parts of the front.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: And it assesses that the Kremlin is very likely using that pause to build up forces for a push north, toward Druzhkivka. That's one of the fortified cities in what's called Ukraine's fortress belt.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: On the battlefield itself, Russian attacks around Kostiantynivka, Borova and Huliaipole on Thursday and Friday didn't gain ground, the Institute says.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: Now an update on yesterday's strikes, and it's a grim one. In Zaporizhzhia, the toll has risen sharply. Yesterday we reported one teenager killed. The Patrol Police now say two people were killed, including that seventeen-year-old boy.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: And the governor, Mykhailo Semikin, says the number of injured has risen to fifty, including eight children. The strikes hit a residential area, including a five-storey apartment building.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: In the Kherson region, local officials reported two people killed and five injured in Russian attacks, with power cut in parts of the city. One person was killed in the Kharkiv region.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: Adding it up, the Kyiv Independent counts at least seven people killed and eighty injured across Ukraine over the day. That includes the two deaths in Odesa we covered yesterday.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: And remember, the same night, a Ukrainian drone attack killed four workers in an industrial zone in Volgograd. So this was a deadly day on both sides, right in the middle of the peace push.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: Let's go to the Gulf. Yesterday's big claim was that Iran's Revolutionary Guards had destroyed an American early-warning radar in Bahrain.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: US Central Command has now denied that publicly. It says the Guards launched two one-way attack drones toward Bahrain, and that American forces shot both down, with no injuries and no damage.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: Neither Bahrain nor any independent source has verified damage. Still, CNN notes it was Iran's first attempt in more than two months to hit a military site in a Gulf state.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: Iran framed it as retaliation for an air attack on a telecom tower in Sirik, on its own coast, which it blamed on an unnamed enemy. And it came the day after President Trump said he'd strike Iran again with no hesitation if it threatened American allies or ships.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: So far, there's been no reported American response beyond shooting down the drones and issuing the denial.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: And the political backdrop has shifted. President Trump posted on Thursday that, quote, we don't need a deal with Iran. That's a change from recent weeks, when he was saying a deal was still possible.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: NPR describes his approach now as keeping things as they are. The blockade stays, the pressure stays, and Qatar keeps trying to bridge the gap.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: Meanwhile, the attacks on shipping haven't stopped. Today the British maritime agency UKMTO reported that a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz was hit by an unknown projectile.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: And separately, Iran's navy said an oil tanker caught fire this morning after hitting a mine in the eastern part of the strait. As with the earlier mine claims, that hasn't been independently verified.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: In Gaza, an Israeli drone strike killed two Palestinians in Jabaliya today. The director of Shifa Hospital says they were walking down a street. The Israeli military says it struck two Hamas militants, and that the results are under review.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: That follows Thursday's strike on Nasser Hospital, where the United Nations reported six killed and twenty-seven injured, and Friday's strike on a vehicle in Deir al-Balah that killed one person.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: And in southern Lebanon on Friday, Israeli artillery shelled five towns while drones flew low over Beirut. No casualties were reported there.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: And between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, the pattern of the week continued on Friday. The Houthis claimed drone attacks on Riyadh's main airport and on a pumping station on the East-West oil pipeline, plus missile fire at Saudi forces in the Jazan region.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: The Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted drones around Riyadh and in the Eastern Region. It hasn't confirmed any hits.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: On the ships, there's nothing new to report. The Theodore Roosevelt is still on its way to the Middle East, with no confirmed position. The George Washington and the George H. W. Bush remain in the Arabian Sea. Monday's USNI fleet tracker should tell us more.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: And a quick number from the site's strike archive. It now holds a hundred and thirty strikes going back to early October, after four were added today and yesterday's Zaporizhzhia entry was revised upward.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: So, what to watch. A date for the prisoner exchange, and for the next round of talks. Whether the Kostiantynivka ceasefire holds, or turns out to be cover for an offensive. And whether Iran tries again after Bahrain.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: That's the briefing. Thanks for listening, and we'll see you tomorrow.
